blocks.p: Then they got up and went on. A little way ahead of them stood an oak, and under it, when they came to it, they found an old pilgrim fast asleep. They knew he was a pilgrim by his clothes, his staff, and his belt.
Great-heart woke him, and the old gentleman, as he opened his eyes, cried out, “What’s the matter? Who are you? What’s your business here?”
“Come, man, don’t be so hot,” said Great-heart. “There’s no one here but friends.”
Still the old man got up and stood on his guard, and wanted to know who they were.
“My name is Great-heart,” said the guide. “I am the guide of these pilgrims, who are going to the Celestial Country.”

“I beg your pardon,” said Mr. Honest. “I was afraid you were some of the company that robbed Little-Faith of his money a while ago. But now that I’ve had a better look at you, I see you’re honester people.”
“Why, what could you have done to help yourself, if we had been that company?”

“Done? I would have fought as long as there was breath in me. And if I had, I’m sure you could never have gotten the better of me; for a Christian can never be overcome unless he gives up of his own accord.”
“Well said, father Honest,” said the guide. “By that I know you’re a cock of the right breed, for you’ve spoken the truth.”
“And by that I know that you know what true pilgrimage is; for everyone else thinks we are the easiest people in the world to overcome.”
“Well, now that we’ve met so happily, may I ask your name, and the name of the place you come from?”
“My name I can’t tell you; but I come from the town of Stupidity. It lies about four degrees beyond the City of Destruction.”
“Oh, are you from that country? Then I think I can half guess who you are. Your name is Old Honesty, isn’t it?”

The old gentleman blushed. “Not Honesty in the abstract,” he said. “Honest is my name, and I hope my nature agrees with what I’m called. But sir, how could you guess that I am such a man, when I come from such a place?”

“I had heard of you before, from my Master, for he knows everything that is done on the earth. But I have often wondered that anyone should come from your town, since it is worse than the City of Destruction itself.”

“Yes, we lie farther from the sun, and so we are colder and more senseless. But if a man were buried in a mountain of ice, and the Sun of Righteousness rose on him, his frozen heart would feel the thaw. And that is how it has been with me.”
“I believe it, father Honest, I believe it; for I know the thing is true.”
Then the old gentleman greeted all the pilgrims with a holy kiss of love, and asked their names, and how they had fared since they set out on their pilgrimage.
“My name I suppose you’ve heard of,” said Christiana. “Good Christian was my husband, and these four are his children.”

You cannot imagine how the old gentleman took it when she told him who she was. He skipped, he smiled, and he blessed them with a thousand good wishes. “I have heard much of your husband,” he said, “and of the travels and wars he went through in his day. Let it be said for your comfort: your husband’s name rings through all these parts of the world. His faith, his courage, his endurance, and his sincerity through it all have made his name famous.”

Then he turned to the boys and asked their names, and they told him. “Matthew,” he said, “be like Matthew the tax collector, not in vice but in virtue. [Matt. 10:3] Samuel, be like Samuel the prophet, a man of faith and prayer. [Ps. 99:6] Joseph, be like Joseph in Potiphar’s house, chaste, and one who runs from temptation. [Gen. 39] And James, be like James the Just, and like James the brother of our Lord.” [Acts 1:13-14]

Then they told him about Mercy, and how she had left her town and her family to come along with Christiana and her sons. At that the honest old man said, “Mercy is your name. By mercy you shall be sustained and carried through every difficulty that assaults you on your way, until you come to the place where you will look the Fountain of Mercy in the face with comfort.”
All this while the guide, Mr. Great-heart, was very pleased, and smiled at his companion.
Now as they walked along together, the guide asked the old gentleman whether he had known one Mr. Fearing, who had come on pilgrimage from his part of the country.
“Yes, very well,” he said. “He was a man who had the root of the matter in him, but he was one of the most troublesome pilgrims I ever met in all my days.”
“I can see you knew him; that’s a very fair portrait of him.”
“Knew him! I was a great companion of his. I was with him most of the time, from when he first began to think about what would come to us hereafter.”
“I was his guide from my Master’s house to the gates of the Celestial City.”
“Then you knew what a troublesome one he was.”
“I did; but I could bear it well enough. Men of my calling are often entrusted with the conduct of people like him.”
“Well then, let’s hear a little about him, and how he managed under your conduct.”

“Why, he was always afraid he would fall short of the place he longed to reach. Everything he heard anyone mention frightened him, if it had the least look of opposition in it. I hear he lay roaring at the Swamp of Despair for about a month together, and wouldn’t venture across, though he saw several go over ahead of him, and though many of them offered him a hand. Yet he wouldn’t go back either. He said he would die if he didn’t reach the Celestial City; and still he was cast down at every difficulty, and stumbled over every straw that anyone threw in his way.

“Well, after he had lain at the swamp a long while, as I told you, one sunny morning he ventured, I don’t know how, and got across; but when he was over, he could hardly believe it. I think he carried a Swamp of Despair in his mind, a swamp he took everywhere with him; otherwise he could never have been the way he was.

“So he came up to the gate, you know the one I mean, at the head of this road; and there too he stood a good while before he dared knock. When the gate was opened, he would step back and let others go ahead, saying he was not worthy. So although he had reached the gate before many of them, many went in ahead of him. There the poor man would stand, shaking and shrinking. I daresay it would have broken your heart to see him; yet he would not go back. At last he took the hammer that hung on the gate in his hand and gave a small rap or two. Then One opened to him, but he shrank back as before. The One who had opened stepped out after him and said, ‘You trembling one, what do you want?’ At that he fell to the ground. The One who spoke to him wondered to see him so faint, and said, ‘Peace be with you. Get up; I have opened the door to you. Come in, for you are blessed.’ So he got up and went in, trembling; and once he was in, he was ashamed to show his face.

“Well, after he had been entertained there a while, as you know is the custom, he was told to go on his way, and shown the road he should take. So he came along until he reached our house. But he behaved at my Master the Interpreter’s door just as he had at the gate. He lay out there in the cold a good while before he would venture to call, yet he wouldn’t go back; and the nights were long and cold then. He even had a letter of need in his pocket to my Master, asking him to receive him and grant him the comfort of his house, and to allow him a stout and valiant guide, because he was so chicken-hearted a man himself. And still, for all that, he was afraid to call at the door. So he hung about the place until, poor man, he was almost starved. So great was his dejection that although he saw several others get in by knocking, he was afraid to try.

“At last, I think it was I who looked out of the window and noticed a man loitering about the door. I went out and asked him who he was; but, poor man, the tears stood in his eyes, so I saw what he wanted. I went in and told the household, and we laid the matter before our Lord. So he sent me out again to beg him to come in; but I can tell you, I had hard work of it. At last he came in; and I will say this for my Lord, he treated him wonderfully lovingly. There were only a few good bits on the table, but some of them were set on his plate. Then he presented his letter, and my Lord looked at it and said his request would be granted.

“So after he had been there a good while, he seemed to take some heart, and to be a little more comfortable; for my Master, you must know, has a very tender heart, especially toward those who are afraid, and so he treated him in whatever way would encourage him most. Well, when he had seen the things of the place and was ready to set out for the City, my Lord gave him, as he had given Christian before him, a bottle of spirits and some comforting things to eat. So we set off, and I went ahead of him; but the man had few words, except that he would sigh out loud.

“When we came to the place where the three fellows were hanged, he said he was afraid that would be his end as well. Only he seemed glad when he saw the Cross and the tomb. There, I admit, he asked to stay a little and look, and for a while afterward he seemed a little cheerier. When we came to the Hill Difficulty he made no fuss about it, nor did he much fear the lions; for you must understand his trouble was not about things like those. His fear was about his acceptance at the end.

“I got him into the House Beautiful, I think, before he was willing. And once he was in, I introduced him to the young women of the place; but he was too ashamed to make much of their company. He wanted very much to be alone, yet he always loved good talk, and often got behind the screen to listen to it. He also loved to look at ancient things, and to ponder them in his mind. He told me afterward that he had loved being in those two houses he had come from last, the gate and the Interpreter’s, but had not dared to be so bold as to say so.

“When we left the House Beautiful, he went down the hill into the Valley of Humiliation as well as I ever saw a man go down in my life; for he did not care how low he was, so long as he might be happy at the last. Indeed, I think there was a kind of sympathy between that valley and him; I never saw him better in all his pilgrimage than when he was there. He would lie down, embrace the ground, and kiss the very flowers that grew in that valley. [Lam. 3:27-29] He was up every morning by daybreak, walking to and fro in it.

“But when he came to the entrance of the Valley of the Shadow of Death, I thought I would lose my man. Not that he had any inclination to go back; he always abhorred that. But he was ready to die of fear. ‘Oh, the hobgoblins will have me! The hobgoblins will have me!’ he cried, and I couldn’t beat it out of him. He made such a noise and outcry there that if they had only heard him, it was enough to encourage them to come and fall on us. But I took special note of this: that valley was as quiet while he went through it as I have ever known it, before or since. I suppose the enemies there had a special check from our Lord just then, and a command not to meddle until Mr. Fearing had passed over.

“It would be too tedious to tell you everything, so I will mention only a passage or two more. When he came to Vanity Fair, I thought he would fight every man in the fair. I was afraid we would both be knocked on the head, so hot was he against their fooleries. On the Enchanted Ground he was very wakeful. But when he came to the river where there is no bridge, there again he was in a sorry state. ‘Now, now,’ he said, ‘I shall be drowned forever, and never see with comfort the Face I have come so many miles to behold.’

“And here too I noticed something remarkable: the water of that river was lower at that time than I ever saw it in all my life. So he got over at last, hardly more than wet-shod. When he was going up to the gate, I began to take my leave of him, and to wish him a good reception above. ‘I shall,’ he said. ‘I shall.’ Then we parted, and I saw him no more.”
“Then it seems he was well at last,” said Honest.

“Yes, yes; I never had any doubt about him. He was a man of a choice spirit, only he was always kept very low, and that made his life so burdensome to himself and so troublesome to others. [Ps. 88] He was, more than most, tender about sin. He was so afraid of doing harm to others that he often denied himself what was lawful, because he would not give offense.” [Rom. 14:21; 1 Cor. 8:13]
“But what could be the reason that such a good man should be so much in the dark all his days?”

“There are two kinds of reasons for it. One is that the wise God will have it so: some must pipe, and some must weep. [Matt. 11:16-18] Now Mr. Fearing was one who played the bass; he and his fellows sound the sackbut, whose notes are more doleful than those of other music; though indeed some say the bass is the ground of all music. For my part, I don’t care at all for a profession of faith that doesn’t begin in heaviness of mind. The first string a musician usually touches is the bass, when he means to bring everything into tune; and God too plays this string first, when he sets a soul in tune for himself. Only here was Mr. Fearing’s imperfection: he could play no other music but this, until toward his latter end.

“I make bold to talk in metaphors like this, to ripen the wits of young readers, and because in the book of Revelation the saved are compared to a company of musicians who play their trumpets and harps and sing their songs before the throne.” [Rev. 8:2; 14:2-3]

“He was a very zealous man, as anyone can see from the account you’ve given,” said Honest. “Difficulties, lions, Vanity Fair, he feared none of them. It was only sin, death, and hell that were a terror to him, because he had some doubts about his share in that celestial country.”

“You’re right. Those were the things that troubled him, and as you’ve rightly noticed, they arose from the weakness of his mind on that point, not from any weakness of spirit as to the practical part of a pilgrim’s life. I’d dare say that, as the proverb goes, he could have bitten a firebrand if it had stood in his way; but the things that oppressed him, no man has ever yet shaken off with ease.”

“This account of Mr. Fearing has done me good,” said Christiana. “I thought no one had ever been like me; but I see there was some likeness between this good man and me. We differed only in two things. His troubles were so great they broke out; mine I kept within. And his pressed on him so hard that he could not knock at the houses provided for entertaining pilgrims; but my trouble always made me knock the louder.”

“If I may speak my heart too,” said Mercy, “I must say that something of him has lived in me as well; for I have always been more afraid of the lake, and of losing a place in Paradise, than of losing anything else. Oh, I thought, if I may only have the happiness of a dwelling there, it is enough, though I part with all the world to win it.”
“Fear was one thing that made me think I was far from having in me what goes along with salvation,” said Matthew. “But if it was so with as good a man as he, why may it not go well with me too?”
“No fears, no grace,” said James. “Though there isn’t always grace where there is fear of hell, it’s certain there’s no grace where there is no fear of God.”

“Well said, James; you’ve hit the mark,” said Great-heart. “For the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, and those who lack the beginning will certainly have neither middle nor end. But we will end our talk of Mr. Fearing here, after we have sent this farewell after him.”

v: Well, Master Fearing, you did fear
And did you fear the lake and pit?
For they who lack your kind of wit

blocks.p: Now I saw that they went on with their talk; for after Great-heart had finished with Mr. Fearing, Mr. Honest began to tell them about another man, whose name was Mr. Self-will. “He claimed to be a pilgrim,” said Honest, “but I am convinced he never came in at the gate that stands at the head of the way.”
“Did you ever talk with him about it?”

“Yes, more than once or twice; but he was always true to his name, self-willed. He cared nothing for man, or argument, or example; whatever his own mind prompted him to do, that he did, and nothing else could he be brought to.”
“And what principles did he hold? I suppose you can tell us.”
“He held that a man might follow the vices of the pilgrims as well as their virtues, and that if he did both, he would certainly be saved.”

“What! If he had said it is possible for the heart to be guilty of the pilgrims’ vices as well as to share in their virtues, he couldn’t much be blamed; for indeed we are exempt from no vice absolutely, but only on condition that we watch and strive. But that, I see, is not what you mean. If I understand you rightly, his opinion was that it was allowable to be so.”
“Yes, yes, that’s what I mean; and so he believed, and so he practiced.”
“But what ground did he have for saying so?”
“Why, he said he had Scripture for his warrant.”
“Please, Mr. Honest, give us a few particulars.”

“I will. He said that David, God’s beloved, had taken other men’s wives, and therefore he could do it. He said that Solomon had kept more women than one, and therefore he could do it. He said that Sarah lied, and the godly midwives of Egypt lied, and so did saved Rahab, and therefore he could do it. He said that the disciples went at their Master’s bidding and took away the owner’s donkey, and therefore he could do that too. He said that Jacob got his father’s inheritance by guile and deception, and therefore so could he.”
“Utterly base! And you’re sure he held this opinion?”
“I’ve heard him plead for it, bring Scripture for it, bring argument for it, and more.”
“An opinion not fit to be tolerated anywhere in the world.”
“You must understand me rightly. He did not say any man might do these things, but that those who had the virtues of the men who did them might do the same.”

“But what conclusion could be more false? That is as much as to say that because good men of old sinned through weakness, he had permission to sin from a presumptuous mind; or that because a child, blown by a gust of wind or stumbling over a stone, fell and dirtied itself in the mud, he might deliberately lie down and wallow in it like a boar. Who could have thought anyone could be so blinded by the power of lust? But what is written must be true: they ‘stumble at the Word, being disobedient, to which also they were appointed.’ [1 Pet. 2:8]

“His supposing that people who give themselves over to the godly men’s vices may still have their virtues is as strong a delusion as the other. It is just as if a dog should say, ‘I have, or may have, the qualities of the child, because I lick up its stinking excrement.’ To eat up the sin of God’s people is no sign of being possessed of their virtues. [Hos. 4:8] Nor can I believe that anyone of this opinion can at present have faith or love in him. But I know you raised strong objections to him. Tell me, what could he say for himself?”
“Why, he said that to do these things openly, as a matter of opinion, seems a great deal more honest than to do them while holding the contrary opinion.”

“A very wicked answer. For though to loosen the bridle on our lusts while our opinions are against such things is bad, to sin and plead a license for it is worse. The one trips up onlookers by accident; the other argues them into the snare.”
“There are many of this man’s mind who don’t have this man’s mouth; and that is what makes going on pilgrimage so little esteemed as it is.”
“You’ve spoken the truth, and it is to be lamented; but he who fears the King of Paradise will come out of them all.”
“There are strange opinions in the world,” said Christiana. “I know one who said it was time enough to repent when they came to die.”
“Such people are not very wise. If that man had a week to run twenty miles for his life, he’d have been very loath to put off the journey to the last hour of the week.”

“You’re right,” said Honest, “and yet most of those who count themselves pilgrims do exactly that. I am, as you see, an old man, and have been a traveler on this road many a day; and I have taken notice of many things.

“I have seen some set out as if they would drive the whole world before them, who yet within a few days died like the Israelites in the wilderness, and never caught sight of the promised land. I have seen some who promised nothing when they first set out as pilgrims, whom you would have thought could not live a day, who yet proved very good pilgrims.
“I have seen some who ran hastily forward, and after a little while ran just as fast back again.

“I have seen some who spoke very well of a pilgrim’s life at first, who after a while spoke just as much against it. I have heard some, when they first set out for Paradise, say positively that there is such a place, who, when they had almost reached it, came back and said there is none.
“I have heard some boast of what they would do if they were opposed, who at a false alarm fled faith, the pilgrim’s way, and everything.”

Now as they were going on their way like this, a man came running to meet them and said, “Gentlemen, and you of the weaker sort, if you love your lives, look to yourselves, for the robbers are ahead of you.”

“Those will be the three who set upon Little-Faith before,” said Great-heart. “Well, we are ready for them.” So they went on their way, and looked around at every turning for where they might meet the villains; but whether the robbers had heard of Mr. Great-heart, or had some other game in view, they never came up to the pilgrims.
